newsitem.title: LAOS: Financing for largest Laos dam hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: Financing for largest Laos dam hangs in balance.

text.p: A senior Lao official on Tuesday argued in favour of building the country's largest dam, as World Bank financing for the $1.5 billion project hung in the balance.
In a rare public hearing on the project, Vice Minister of Industry and Handicraft Khammone Phonekeo pleaded for implementation of the delayed Nam Theun 2 (NT2) dam project.
"The project ranks among the first priorities for the social and economic development of the country," he told participants, who included government officials, developers and the World Bank.
The dam is to be built on the Nakai Plateau, about 250 km (155 km) east of Vientiane in central Laos.
But some were sceptical that the dam would benefit the country's economy and questioned why developers were unwilling to proceed with the project.
They also noted that the power to be produced by the project had no buyer.

A 1995 power purchase agreement with the Electricity Authority of Thailand (EGAT) expired when the Nam Theun 2 Electricity Consortium (NTEC) could not complete the project by 2000 as originally promised.

"Everything rises and falls on whether EGAT buys the electricity," said one participant at the meeting. "No one seems to be taking seriously the fact that Thailand doesn't necessarily have to buy this power."

Laos signed a memorandum of understanding with EGAT to supply 3,000 megawatts of power by 2009, and plans 18 dams to meet Thailand's need for electricity. But there is no existing agreement for purchasing power from NT2.

Lao government officials told participants they were confident EGAT would support the project, and the authors of an upcoming report on the dam's financial viability were also confident that EGAT would buy NT2 power.

NTEC, which represents the developers -- Australia-based Transfield Corp, Electricite de France, Thailand's Jasmine International, Italian-Thai Development Plc, and Thailand's Phatra Thanakit Plc -- is also depending on EGAT to be the buyer.
But the delays have driven up the cost of NT2, leading some to question how the impoverished Lao government can afford a 25 percent stake in a $1.5 billion project.
Project officials said a refusal by the World Bank to provide $100 million in partial loan guarantees could derail the project.
The World Bank said it will not make a decision on those loans until it has more information from this and other public consultations and studies on the economic and environmental impacts of the dam.
Reacting to an apparent boycott of the meeting by non-governmental organisations, Lao officials said they would hold another meeting for those organisations to demonstrate that the process was open.
